newsitem.title: UK: UK tax credit crackdown too harsh - tax experts.
newsitem.headline: UK tax credit crackdown too harsh - tax experts.

text.p: A British government decision to abolish tax credits for share buybacks and special dividends was too harsh, tax experts said on Tuesday.
The timing of the move was directly linked to Reuters Holdings Plc's share buyback plans which were due to be put to shareholders on Wednesday, Roger Muray, tax partner at Ernst & Young, said.
Following the government announcement, Reuters announced it would delay consideration of plans to return 613 million stg to shareholders via a buyback and special bonus dividend issue.
"The timing is no coincidence...it's crystal clear that it's aimed at Reuters special dividend shares," Muray said, adding that the ruling would have wide-ranging effects.
"I think it's overkill to apply it to share buybacks...it creates an impediment to companies trying to reduce their capital," he said.
John Whiting, tax partner at Price Waterhouse, agreed that the government's decison on tax credits, which took immediate effect on Tuesday, was unfair in several aspects.
"I think it's unfair to affect plans already announced under the law before today. It would have been fairer if it had applied only to new schemes," Whiting said.
"I'm sure it'll reduce the number of buybacks," he added.
Reuters is just one of a growing number of cash-rich British companies to have announced plans to return money to shareholders via a buyback and special dividend.
So far British companies have spent 2.5 billion stg on share buybacks this year with four billion stg expected by end 1996.
The major beneficiaries of share buybacks involving special dividends are tax-exempt investors such as pension funds.
A proliferation in these deals has sharply increased the cost to the government and prompted the clampdown which it is estimated will save up to 400 million stg a year from 1998-99.

Tax experts said the move would impede share buybacks for heavily-capitalised companies seeking to reduce capital and would also limit a company's flexibility to table a special dividend as a form of sweetener in a takeover bid.
"Companies will be frustrated, especially banks who are trying to reduce capital," said Muray.
However, Barclays Plc which has already carried out three share buybacks, said it would continue to use share repurchases as a mechanism for managing its equity capital.

Special dividends benefit companies and shareholders in two ways. A company issuing a special dividend has to pay Advance Corporation Tax (ACT) which it can offset against corporation tax, particularly useful for companies which derive a high proportion of earnings in Britain.
The tax-exempt shareholder not only has the benefit of the special dividend payout but also receives additional payment in the form of a tax credit, making such deals doubly attractive.
Muray argued that by abolishing the tax credit an element of double taxation is introduced as the company and the shareholder both pay tax. "Buybacks will be penalised in future," he said.
Price Waterhouse's Whiting suggested that companies seeking alternative ways to return cash to shareholders may opt to increase the ordinary dividend on a one-off basis instead.

Experts agree that central to the debate is a definition of a "special dividend'. The British tax authorities said that tax treatment of special dividends not linked to share consolidations or takeovers remained unchanged but tax experts called for greater clarification on this point.
"It's 'tainted' special diivdends they are targetting...we may see more interest in Foreign Income Dividends (FIDS)," Murray said.
FIDs carry a notional lower rate of income tax which is not repayable and does not attract a tax credit but can be offset against tax liability, a tax authority spokeswoman said.
Looking ahead, Muray said Tuesday's move implied that ACT would not be scrapped in the British budget on November 26.
